newsitem.title: USA: Don't root for cute in looney 'ToonStruck'.
newsitem.headline: Don't root for cute in looney 'ToonStruck'.

text.p: Brace yourselves. It takes a mighty strong stomach to play "ToonStruck" (DOS/Windows95, $55).

It's not that this CD-ROM game from Virgin Interactive is violent or perverted. (Well, actually, it is a wee bit perverted). The problem is that you may feel sick if you spend too much time with the overly adorable creatures of Cutopia, which serves as the setting for much of this story.

"ToonStruck" is the tale of Drew Blanc, a writer for "The Fluffy Fluffy Bun Bun Show," where Fluffy Fluffy Bun Bun and his pals are sappier than Care Bears on Prozac. Drew has just been told by his production boss that he has until morning to come up with a new show that's even cuter.

At 4 a.m., a freak accident teleports Drew into the cartoon world of Cutopia, where the king is one of those big yellow smiley faces, there are "carecrows" instead of scarecrows, and the local video arcade's most popular game is "Sweet Fighter 2," where players hurl compliments at their opponents.

There's trouble in Cutopia. The ruler of the other half of the island, Count Nefarious, has created The Malevolator, which shoots beams that transform chunks of Cutopia and its inhabitants into dark, twisted versions of themselves.

King Smiley Face Person agrees to help Drew find a way back to his world if he first helps the kingdom's scientist find parts to The Cutifier, an invention designed to undo the damage caused by The Malevolator.
The real wonder of this game is that Drew doesn't start rooting for Count Nefarious, especially after the palace guards, Sparky and Chipper, insist on doing the hideous "Hello dance."
Fortunately, all is not sweetness and light.

Drew is joined on his quest by the sarcastic Flux Wildly, and his pilgrimage takes him to the adjacent island of Zanydu, where he must confront an obnoxious security guard, a bodybuilding instructor and some bowlers with some very unorthodox techniques for knocking down pins.

And when he gets to the Malevolands, Drew gets to meet a maniacal clown who loves to torture balloon animals and the dim-witted, hyperallergic Snout, who sounds like a flight attendant as he announces, "I'll be your merciless dungeon guard for the rest of your stay."

Presiding over this madness is actor Christopher Lloyd, best known for his "Back to the Future" roles and that of Judge Doom in "Who Framed Roger Rabbit?" Tim Curry, Dom DeLuise and Dan Castellaneta also lend their voices to the characters.

At times, "ToonStruck" seems to be a game in search of an audience. The first part has moments that are unbearably sappy but once you get past those scenes, it's clear that this cartoon is not for children.
It's rated for teenagers, and the box says it's because of the "mild animated violence" and "comic mischief." But it's also for the sexual double entendres and the bathroom humour.
If you can ignore the blather, "ToonStruck" will keep you busy for days. And if you like your games off-beat and a little off-colour, this is one toon you'd be loony not to try.
Some new and notable software in the stores this week:

"Leisure Suit Larry: Love for Sail!" (Sierra, Windows/DOS, $40) -- The computer world's most loveably luckless lounge lizard is back, on a cruise ship filled with "more beauties than Mother Nature can make; or Dow Corning." You can try to get friendly with characters like Dewmi Moore and Captain Thygh, or attempt a menage a twang with sisters Wydoncha and Nailmi Jugg. It's for ages 17 and older.

"Tom Clancy SSN" (Simon & Schuster Interactive, Windows95, $60) -- A simulation where you command the nuclear attack submarine USS Cheyenne for 15 missions. The underlying crisis: a Chinese takeover of the oil-rich Spratly Islands.

"Tomb Raider" (Eidos Interactive, Windows95/DOS, $50) -- This Indiana Jones-style game uses a heroine with a Barbie doll waist and a Pamela Anderson bust to stand out in the crowded field of adventure products. Also available on PlayStation, it's for ages 13 and older.

"They Call Me . . . The Skul" and "The Suit" (Byron Preiss Multimedia, Windows, $20) is based on two comic books from Virtual Comics. Skul is a teenager with an apparent spelling problem who has been framed for his girlfriend's murder and gets his superpowers from a mysterious tattoo. The Suit, which has nothing to do with corporate executives, involves armoured suits that burn out the person wearing them. There's a computerized comic book and arcade game for each title.

"Pie Jackers" (Windows95, $30) is a 23rd century cartoon race to deliver pizza pies. It stars the voices of Cheech Martin and Cyndi Lauper. Simon & Schuster Interactive bills this as "the cheesiest racing game ever." It's difficult to know if this is a cute description or a real warning.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
